notes: STAND-IN (read as its own source, not used to confirm the article): Duarte, C. M. 1987, PhD thesis, McGill University (docs/research_notes/fetched/v2/Duarte_1987.pdf), chapter I 'Patterns in biomass and cover of aquatic macrophytes in lakes'. Read on page images (docs/research_notes/fetched/v2/Duarte_etal_1986.thesis1987-p20.png, -p27.png, -p29.png, -p33.png): Table 1.1 (printed p. 16, PDF p. 29) gives mean %Am 44.1 (n 104), %As 35.0 (n 82), %Ae 12.3 (n 77), each ranging 0–100 % — the percent of lake area covered by all macrophytes, submerged and emergent plants. The data set (printed p. 14, PDF p. 27) 'included 139 lakes': Europe 58, North America 62, Africa 6, South Africa 4, Asia 6, Australia 1 (Table 1.1's lake-area row has N = 141). The chapter abstract (printed p. 7, PDF p. 20) says underwater light 'was found to be the best descriptor of the cover and biomass of submerged plants'. Table 1.3 (printed p. 20, PDF p. 33): eq. (1) ln As = 0.91 ln A − 1.1 (R² 0.80, N 76); eq. (3) ln As = 0.94 ln A + 0.85 ln Iz − 3.7 (R² 0.89, N 51); eq. (7) %As = 1.4 Iz + 0.07 Lic − 24 Sal − 0.90 (R² 0.60, N 55), with A in ha, Iz the annual irradiance at the mean depth and Lic the days of ice cover. Check of the paper's ~20 %: eq. 1 gives %As = 100·e^−1.1·A^−0.09 = 22.0 % at 100 ha, 20.7 % at 200 ha and 19.9 % at 300 ha — consistent. Recommendation: the thesis supports all three claims; cite it alongside, or read the article (doi:10.1139/f86-235) before confirming. The same chapter also notes that submerged cover is proportionally smaller in larger lakes, partly because larger lakes are deeper (R² 0.41 between lake size and mean depth).
